Binary search works by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half.  
To decide which half to continue searching, the algorithm compares the target value with the middle element of the current interval.  
This comparison can only reliably eliminate one half of the remaining data if the elements are **ordered** (either ascending or descending).  
If the data are unsorted, the middle element gives no information about whether the target lies to its left or right, so the algorithm cannot discard a portion of the search space and may miss the target or loop indefinitely.  
Therefore, binary search requires the input collection to be sorted beforehand.
